corpus.signal_text:

            US, China to open AI ‘communication channel’
  - AFP, WASHINGTON
 The US and China agreed to set up a “communication channel” for artificial intelligence (AI) incidents, the White House said on Friday, after a Washington summit short on breakthroughs. US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) discussed matters ranging from AI and trade to the stalled war in Iran, and confirmed that they would meet for a third and fourth time this year at international summits in China and the US. Xi’s visit to Washington was marked more by pomp than substance, but the White House said the nations agreed to establish a “bilateral communication channel” for AI incidents. US President Donald Trump, right, speaks with Chinese President Xi Jinping on the steps of the US National Archives Museum in Washington on Friday.Photo: AP While billionaire Trump has repeatedly dismissed fears that AI could pose a threat to humanity, Xi took a more measured tone, saying that the technology must develop under human control. The White House also reported some deals from the visit, including China agreeing to import at least 10 million tonnes of coal from the US next year and in 2028. Additionally, the two countries agreed more favorable tariff treatment for US$30 billion of “non-sensitive goods” in each direction and two Chinese pandas were to arrive at a US zoo. Beijing did not immediately comment after the White House statements.

corpus.title: China and US announce AI safety channel even as Trump claims ‘super intelligence’ needs no guardrails
corpus.signal_text:
China and US announce AI safety channel even as Trump claims ‘super intelligence’ needs no guardrails
Xi Jinping reportedly told his US counterpart that AI must be harnessed ‘for good’, despite Trump calling safety fears a hoax

The US and China agreed to set up a channel for handling artificial intelligence (AI)-related incidents, according to an announcement at the end of their three-day summit, even though president Donald Trump has claimed the technology doesn’t need any new guardrails.
Xi Jinping's first visit to the White House produced no major breakthroughs, but experts say it provided them an opportunity to nurture cooperation and set up working groups that could prevent problems from escalating.
The White House on Saturday said both sides would set up a communication mechanism for AI-related incidents, to discuss related risks and benefits, with further AI-specific talks scheduled for November.
During their summit, Mr Xi reportedly told Mr Trump that both nations can and must develop and manage AI “for good”, in contrast to the American president’s stance that safety fears over the technology are “a hoax”.
Mr Xi told Mr Trump: “Both China and the United States are leading nations in artificial intelligence. [We must] ensure that the development of AI is always under human control and serves the wellbeing of the people.”
AI bosses in recent weeks have sounded alarm over the potential of the technology to threaten the future of the human race. Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI maker ChatGPT, said the world was right to be afraid of AI, and the warnings have led to new calls for regulation of the technology.
Two researchers from Anthropic, the company behind the advanced AI assistant Claude, also warned this month that the rapidly progressing technology could lead to the extinction of the human race in the not-too-distant future.
It prompted the UN human rights chief to ask AI companies to rein in development of the technology, cautioning that the world was “on the cusp of irreversible change" that could affect generations of humanity.
But at the UN General Assembly last Tuesday, Mr Trump dismissed calls for stricter controls, branding the warnings “a hoax”.
